query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-heating the substrate during selective laser melting (SLM) of high-entropy alloy components will reduce the steep thermal gradients that cause residual stresses and defects, thereby enhancing dimensional precision and mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐manufactured high-entropy alloy components (e.g., CoCrFeNiMn) produced by SLM at room temperature, which typically exhibit rapid cooling, high residual stress, hot cracking, porosity, and dimensional distortions.
generation.intervention: Implement a substrate pre-heating step (e.g., tuning the build platform temperature into an optimal range, approximately 200–400 °C) during the SLM process.
generation.conditions: The intervention applies under standard SLM processing conditions with identical laser power, scan strategies, powder feedstock, and inert atmosphere; the alloy system is a typical HEA such as CoCrFeNiMn used for complex geometries.
generation.structural_mediator: By reducing the temperature differential between the molten pool and the substrate, pre-heating moderates the cooling rate and thermal gradients, leading to lower residual stresses, improved grain coalescence, and fewer fabrication-induced defects (e.g., porosity and hot cracks).
generation.mechanism: The reduced thermal gradient from substrate pre-heating slows down the solidification process, which minimizes abrupt contraction and internal stress buildup; this permits a more uniform microstructure and dimensional stability by limiting residual stress–induced deformations and defect formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to parts built without pre-heating, components fabricated with substrate pre-heating are predicted to exhibit improved dimensional fidelity, lower defect densities, and enhanced mechanical properties such as higher yield strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: SLM-fabricated HEA components produced under conventional (room temperature) substrate conditions that typically show significant residual stress, defects (e.g., porosity and hot cracking), and dimensional inaccuracies.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected within an optimal pre-heating temperature window; temperatures exceeding the optimal range might introduce oxidation or other deleterious thermal effects. The benefit will also depend on the specific alloy composition and SLM parameters.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements (e.g., percentage reduction in defect density or enhancement in mechanical properties) and the optimum pre-heating temperature require further experimental calibration for each HEA system.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical HEA components (e.g., CoCrFeNiMn) using SLM: one set with substrate pre-heating (within the 200–400 °C range) and a control set without pre-heating. Use identical laser parameters, powder characteristics, and build geometries in an inert atmosphere.
measurements: Dimensional accuracy measured using coordinate metrology tools
Residual stress assessment via X-ray diffraction or other stress-analysis techniques
Defect density evaluation using microscopy (or CT scanning) to quantify porosity and crack incidence
Mechanical properties tested through tensile testing (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-heated samples do not show statistically significant improvements (e.g., less than a 5% improvement in dimensional precision, defect reduction, or mechanical properties) compared to the control group, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Laser metal deposition (LMD) is a type of laser additive manufacturing technology. When integrated with robotic arms, it enables the fabrication of complex components, and unlike SLM technology, it is not constrained by the volume limitations of the working chamber [,,]. Therefore, in this study, LMD was employed to fabricate AlFeCoCrNi2.1 EHEA components, with as-casting AlFeCoCrNi2.1 samples serving as reference materials. The systematic investigation of the effects of heat treatment on microstructures aims to enrich the understanding of the heat treatment–microstructure–mechanical property relationships in the field of EHEA components fabricated via AM.

This study uniquely demonstrates the processability, hot-cracking susceptibility, and in situ mechanical response of CoCrFeNiCu-HEA fabricated by L-PBF, providing new insights into defect evolution and mechanical performance under these specific processing conditions. Future work will focus on targeted alloying (e.g., Al addition), pre-heating strategies, and optimized scanning to further reduce hot-cracking susceptibility and enhance mechanical performance. This study provides insights into the processability, defect evolution, and mechanical response of L-PBF CoCrFeNiCu-HEA, guiding the development of crack-resistant, additively manufactured HEAs.

AbstractThe equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy (HEA) possesses excellent properties including exceptional strength–ductility synergy, high corrosion resistance, and good thermal stability. Selective laser melting (SLM) additive manufacturing facilitates the convenient fabrication of the CoCrFeNiMn HEA parts with complex geometries. Here, the SLM process optimization was conducted to achieve a high relative density of as-built CoCrFeNiMn HEA bulks. The mechanisms of process-induced defects and process control were elucidated. The microscale mechanical behaviors were analyzed through in situ scanning electron microscopy observation during the compression tests on micro-pillars of the as-built HEA. The stress–strain characteristics by repeated slip and mechanism of “dislocation avalanche” during the compression of micro-pillars were discussed. The high-cycle fatigue tests of the as-built HEA were performed. It was found that a large number of nano-twins were induced by the fatigue, causing a non-negligible cycle softening phenomenon.
